header:
Date: 2026-12-31 | Time: 15:00 UTC | Duration: 52m
Attendees: Alex Kim (Redwood AE), Priya Desai (Redwood SE), Marta Lopez (ClearSight CTO), Daniel Reed (ML Eng), Samir Khan (Head of DevOps)
summary: POC scoping focused on benchmark planning and integrating customer inference scripts into Redwood's benchmark harness. Discussed success criteria (latency SLAs, cost per token, quality/regression thresholds), workload sizing (prompt/token distributions, RPS/concurrency), and test matrix covering streaming vs non-streaming modes. Agreed next steps: share harness repo, customer to provide scripts and prompt sets, schedule load run, and SE to draft test matrix and resource estimates.
topics: Success criteria: 95th pct latency, cost targets, quality thresholds
Workload sizing: average/peak RPS, token lengths, concurrency
Benchmark harness integration: how to plug in customer scripts, runners, metrics collected
Streaming vs non-streaming: measurement differences, instrumentation
Dedicated vs Hosted tradeoffs for throughput and isolation
transcript:
[00:00] Alex Kim: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, um, we're here to scope the POC around the benchmark harness integration.
[00:07] Marta Lopez: Yep thanks, excited — a lot riding on this for our roadmap. We need to make sure performance and cost line up.
[00:13] Priya Desai: Quick intro from our side, I'm Priya, Solutions Eng at Redwood, I'll run the benchmarks with you and help integrate your scripts.
[00:20] Daniel Reed: Great, Daniel here. We have a few existing inference scripts in Python — simple gRPC-ish clients, and some internal wrappers.
[00:27] Alex Kim: Perfect. High level goals: 1) validate latency SLOs in both streaming and non-streaming modes, 2) measure cost per million tokens and compare against your current infra, 3) ensure model quality doesn't regress on youreval set.
[00:41] Samir Khan: For us security is big — VPC peering or private deployment may be required. We also need to understand audit logs and KMS integration.
[00:50] Priya Desai: Noted. We'll include a security checklist. For the bench harness, we typically accept customer scripts two ways: you can drop in your Python runner that hits Redwood's test endpoint, or we can wrap your inference function with our harness adapter. The harness is a small Python tool + a load runner (we use vegeta/gunicorn-ish for non-streaming; for streaming we use a streaming harness that measures partial tokens and tail latency).
[01:12] Daniel Reed: Sounds good. Our scripts currently do streaming websocket calls and also have a non-streaming REST path.
[01:18] Alex Kim: That's ideal — we can exercise both. A couple of clarifying Qs: What's your average prompt size and peak RPS?
[01:25] Daniel Reed: Average prompt about 250 tokens, responses avg ~180 tokens. Baseline is 5 RPS, peak bursts 20 RPS sustained for a few minutes, concurrency around 10 clients.
[01:38] Priya Desai: Ok, we'll set test scenarios: baseline 5 RPS, peak 20 RPS, and an endurance run at 10 RPS for 30 minutes. We'll measure latency p50/p95/p99, tokens/sec, throughput, and cost per million tokens.
[01:51] Marta Lopez: Success criteria from our side — p95 < 500ms for non-streamed short completions, streaming tail latency such that user-perceived time < 700ms, and regression in our quality eval < 1.5% drop. Also cost target roughly <= $150 per 1M tokens (ballpark).
[02:07] Alex Kim: We'll map those to the test matrix. Note: streaming numbers are inherently different — we'll capture first-byte, incremental-token latency, and end-to-end.
[02:16] Samir Khan: On infra: will the test run from Redwood's hosted infra or our VPC? We need to validate networking egress and any firewall rules.
[02:24] Priya Desai: We can run both. For an initial run we'll use Redwood hosted regions in us-west-2, then we can run a private run in your VPC or Dedicated pool to measure isolation effects. We'll need a small peering window.
[02:36] Daniel Reed: Regarding data, we can't send PHI to hosted endpoints. We'll provide synthetic but representative prompts.
[02:42] Alex Kim: Understood — synthetic is fine as long as token distribution and prompt complexity match.
[02:47] Priya Desai: Integration detail: please share your Python client code and a sample requirements.txt. We'll add our harness adapter with two entry points: run_streaming.py and run_nonstream.py. The harness will emit metrics to Prometheus and a CSV summary.
[03:02] Daniel Reed: Any changes needed in our scripts? We prefer minimal changes; maybe a small adapter function.
[03:07] Priya Desai: Exactly — we typically ask for a simple call signature: send_prompt(prompt) -> generator OR response object. We'll wrap it if needed.
[03:13] Marta Lopez: Bench comparisons — we'd like to see Dedicated GPU vs Hosted numbers. Can you estimate resources?
[03:19] Priya Desai: We'll produce a resource estimate after initial junes — sorry, the initial run. Typical guidance: for your workload (avg 430 tokens per request) we expect ~X throughput per A100-equivalent instance; we'll provide both quantized and fp16 profiles. We'll also show batching effects.
[03:33] Alex Kim: Tradeoffs: batching reduces cost but increases latency; prefix/KV cache can significantly cut tokens-per-inference for chat workflows. We'll include cache on/off tests.
[03:43] Samir Khan: How do you measure model quality? We need reproducible evals.
[03:48] Priya Desai: Provide an eval set and rubric — we'll run BLEU/ROUGE-style metric or your custom classifier. We'll also run A/B comparisons between model versions to detect regressions.
[03:58] Daniel Reed: For streaming vs non-streaming, what metrics should we expect?
[04:02] Priya Desai: For streaming: time-to-first-byte, tokens/sec, incremental latency between token chunks, end-to-end. For non-streaming: request latency p50/p95/p99 and throughput. We'll also capture server-side GPU utilization and memory.
[04:16] Alex Kim: Example test matrix rows: streaming small (avg 50 tokens) baseline, streaming long (avg 400 tokens) peak, non-streaming short, non-streaming long, cache-hit scenario, cache-miss scenario.
[04:28] Marta Lopez: Timeline — we want a pilot run in the first two weeks of January. Is that feasible?
[04:33] Priya Desai: Yes. Action plan: Alex will send the harness repo and quickstart today/tomorrow, Daniel supplies prompt sets by end of next week, then we schedule a 2-hour full load test the week of Jan 11. SE will draft the exact test matrix by Jan 3.
[04:47] Samir Khan: One more on compliance — do you provide SOC2 docs and logs for proof?
[04:52] Alex Kim: Yes we can share SOC2 and ISO artifacts through our security portal; for Private deployments we support KMS/HSM and full audit logs.
[04:59] Daniel Reed: Ok, any blockers?
[05:01] Alex Kim: The only dependencies are: we need the sample scripts and the token distribution; confirm whether the pilot uses hosted endpoints or a Dedicated trial; and network peering window if you want VPC test.
[05:12] Priya Desai: We'll also need to confirm which model you want us to run — open model variant or a Redwood-curated profile. That affects quantization/latency.
[05:20] Marta Lopez: We'll start with the lighter open model to get baseline and then compare with a higher quality model.
[05:25] Alex Kim: Great. Recap next steps and action items...
[05:28] Priya Desai: Recap: 1) Alex share harness + README, 2) Daniel provide prompts and scripts, 3) Priya produce test matrix, 4) Samir confirm networking.
[05:36] Marta Lopez: Sounds good, thanks everyone.
[05:38] Alex Kim: Thanks, we'll follow up with calendar invite for the load run.
[05:41] [call ends]
